title: Car payments hit $840, but a bigger warning is emerging
summary: New car payments are climbing faster than vehicle prices.
content: Another affordability shock awaits American car buyers. Even as automakers offer more discounts, new car monthly payments are reaching record levels in November. J.D. Power and GlobalData forecast that the average new-vehicle payment will reach $840 in November, up 4.2% from a year earlier. Average transaction prices are expected to climb 2.2% to $47,154, setting another November record. A concerning disparity is highlighted by the estimate, which was made public on November 19: Monthly payments are increasing at almost twice the rate of car costs. The strain is being increased by higher borrowing rates. It is anticipated that the average new-car loan rate would hit 6.71%, the highest level since November of 2023. However, the financial burden goes beyond monthly expenses. About one-third of cars traded in November are expected to have negative equity, meaning owners owe more on their loans than the cars are worth. Meanwhile, an increasing number of purchasers are extending loans to seven years or more to make payments more bearable. Americans still buy cars in spite of these obstacles. After accounting for selling days, November sales are expected to total around 1.2 million, a 1.2% rise over the previous year. For consumers, the figures raise a difficult question: Are Americans finding ways to afford increasingly expensive cars, or simply taking on more debt? New car payments reach a troubling November record J.D. Power’s forecast shows that financing costs continue to increase, despite growing manufacturer incentives. Fuel costs and high borrowing rates are two of the greatest obstacles to car affordability, according to Thomas King, head of OEM Solutions at J.D. Power. According to the forecast, several indicators highlight the financial pressure facing buyers: Average monthly payment: $840, up 4.2% year over year Average transaction price: $47,154, up 2.2% Average loan interest rate: 6.71%, up 0.61 percentage points Trade-ins with negative equity: 30.3%, up 0.7 percentage points Loans lasting 84 months or longer: 12.8%, up 1.1 percentage points Average manufacturer incentives: $3,589 per vehicle, up 5.6% J.D. Power published the figures in its November automotive forecast, which also projected rising inventories at dealerships. The numbers suggest that rising borrowing costs are not entirely covered by discounts. Consumers are allocating a larger portion of their monthly budgets to car payments, despite manufacturers offering incentives. A record number of buyers face another debt problem Negative equity is perhaps the most alarming trend. J.D. Power projects that 30.3% of vehicle trade-ins in November will be underwater, meaning the outstanding loan balance exceeds the vehicle’s value. The leftover amount may need to be paid separately or added to the financing on a new car if the debt exceeds the vehicle’s value. When that debt is rolled over into a new loan, the amount borrowed increases, along with the total amount of interest paid. Longer financing durations are also becoming more common. J.D. Power expects 12.8% of new-vehicle loans to carry terms of at least 84 months, equivalent to seven years. Longer loans may lower monthly payments, but they usually result in higher overall borrowing costs and may leave borrowers with longer-term debt that exceeds the value of their cars. For families already juggling high vehicle payments, the combination of negative equity and longer lending periods poses a serious problem. New car payments hit $840 as another warning emerges. Oscar Wong / Getty Images Kelley Blue Book reveals another troubling car price record Additional statistics from Kelley Blue Book show the larger issue of cost. Cox Automotive reported Nov. 10 that average new-vehicle transaction prices reached $51,109 in October, an all-time high and a 2.1% increase from a year earlier. Since J.D. Power’s November estimate and the October Kelley Blue Book number use different datasets and methodology, they shouldn’t be directly compared from month to month. The average price reported by Kelley Blue Book increased as a result of expensive SUVs and pickup trucks. But more reasonably priced car sectors still exist. According to the survey, the average October transaction prices for small cars were $28,030, while those for small SUVs were $37,895. Why car buyers are still spending despite higher payments Even amid rising borrowing costs, November vehicle demand remains relatively resilient. J.D. Power and GlobalData forecast approximately 996,200 retail vehicle sales during November, up 1.6% on a selling-day-adjusted basis. To sustain demand, manufacturers are also raising incentives. The average car discount is expected to be $3,589, which is about $235 higher than in October. With their proportion of retail sales predicted to reach 18.3%, up three percentage points from the previous year, hybrid cars are becoming more popular. Electric vehicles are projected to account for 6.7% of retail sales. The ongoing demand indicates that despite affordability constraints, Americans are still buying cars. Longer loan terms and growing negative equity, however, suggest that some purchasers are depending on more intricate financing arrangements. Comparing the overall cost of the car, interest rate, and length of the loan may be more important to prospective buyers than concentrating only on monthly payments. Although a reduced monthly fee may seem appealing, it does not always indicate that a car is more reasonably priced. Related: Nvidia’s $270 Wall Street upgrade has a surprising catch

title: Chinese cars face new U.S. roadblock as prices soar
summary: A powerful union is pushing Congress to tighten restrictions on Chinese automakers.
content: The cost of new cars is at an all-time high for Americans. Congress should now make it much more difficult for Chinese automakers to join the U.S. market, according to a strong labor union. Reuters reported Nov. 24 that the International Brotherhood of Teamsters urged lawmakers to pass tougher restrictions on Chinese vehicles before Congress adjourns for the year. The union, which represents about 1.3 million workers, contends that Chinese automakers pose a danger to local companies, American manufacturing employment, and national security. The campaign comes as Americans continue to worry about affordability. Kelley Blue Book reported Nov. 10 that average new-vehicle transaction prices reached a record $51,109 in October, up 2.1% from a year earlier. Chinese automakers, such as BYD and Geely, have grown globally by producing cars at a variety of price points. However, U.S. tariffs and connected-vehicle regulations create significant obstacles to their entry. The proposed legislation would codify existing limitations into federal law and strengthen them. That begs the question for American consumers: Could protecting domestic manufacturing reduce competition that could lower car prices? Teamsters push Congress for tougher Chinese car restrictions Teamsters President Sean O’Brien urged senators to pass the Connected Vehicle Security Act of 2026, claiming that Chinese manufacturers might jeopardize national security and hurt American companies. O’Brien’s letter demanded limitations before legislators depart Washington for the year, according to Reuters . Bipartisan legislation sponsored by Senators Bernie Moreno (R-Ohio) and Elissa Slotkin (D-Mich.) restricts vehicles and technology from China while addressing other national security threats. The Teamsters endorsed the proposal in May, warning that Chinese manufacturers could undercut American workers and eliminate union jobs. The Commerce Department’s current restrictions are expanded upon by the bill. The Bureau of Industry and Security says its rules prohibit sales of covered Chinese- and Russian-linked connected vehicles and software beginning with model year 2027. Restrictions on specified connectivity hardware begin with model year 2030. That foundation would be strengthened by the new legislation, which would also make reversals more difficult in the future. Moreno expressed optimism that legislators will soon come to a consensus, according to Reuters. The bill has not yet been signed into law. Record car prices sharpen the affordability debate The October results from Kelley Blue Book demonstrate the financial strain that American auto purchasers are under. While the average manufacturer’s recommended retail price hit $52,933, the average new-car transaction price increased 1.3% from September to $51,109. Incentives averaged 6.8% of transaction prices, equivalent to approximately $3,490 per vehicle. The record average was influenced by pricey SUVs and pickup vehicles. Nonetheless, buyers persisted in acquiring more reasonably priced automobiles. On average, small cars cost $28,030, while compact SUVs cost $37,895. There are conflicting agendas in the discussion of Chinese imports. Restrictions, according to supporters, save American employment from unfair competition by manufacturers that profit from Chinese industrial practices. Restrictive trade policy opponents argue that keeping out possible rivals might reduce customer choice and lessen pressure on local automakers to cut costs. However, more stringent regulations wouldn’t always result in price increases right once. There are already significant obstacles preventing Chinese passenger cars from entering the U.S. market. The longer-term issue is whether restricting future competition will affect affordability. A new U.S. car ban could have an unexpected consequence. Kevin Dietsch / Getty Images Mercedes-Benz and Volvo complicate the proposed ban The law may also affect manufacturers with complicated foreign ownership structures or Chinese investors. Reuters reported that Chinese investors hold approximately 20% of Mercedes-Benz, including stakes associated with BAIC Group and Geely Chairman Li Shufu. A Senate committee version of the legislation would restrict certain automakers with Chinese ownership exceeding 15%. According to Moreno, legislators are considering compromise clauses to prevent China’s Geely Holding, which owns the bulk of Mercedes-Benz and Volvo, from being barred from the U.S. market. The law also covers hardware and software for connected vehicles, which may have an impact on producers outside of China. The Senate Commerce Committee’s report outlines restrictions, enforcement procedures, and exemptions. Compliance for well-established firms may include examining foreign business partnerships, ownership structures, and suppliers. What happens next for American drivers? The proposal still has to be approved by Congress, and talks may result in changes to its final parameters. Since significant limitations currently restrict such imports, American buyers won’t witness an immediate shift in the availability of Chinese vehicles for the time being. But in the coming years, the law may impact which suppliers, producers, and technologies enter the U.S. market. The Teamsters frame the issue as safeguarding national security and American jobs. Another worry for drivers currently facing record-high auto costs is whether more competition will eventually be sacrificed to support local manufacturers. title: Fed rate-hike bets deliver fresh blow to your holiday budget
summary: Hot PCE inflation, new tariff proposals strengthen expectations for a December rate hike and more price increases in 2027.
content: American households are getting squeezed from all sides this holiday season as stubborn inflation and a stronger-than-expected U.S. economy collide with a fresh wave of proposed tariffs. For America’s consumers and borrowers, their money worries are no longer just a single interest-rate hike in December but perhaps a relentless tightening cycle that could push the Federal Reserve to keep raising the benchmark federal funds rate through January, March, and possibly beyond before rate cuts could resume in 2028. “Additional tariffs complicate the inflation situation along with the lingering ways in which supply chains have been roiled due to the AI buildout, KPMG Chief Economist and Managing Director Diane Swonk said in a blog post. “The Fed is in a tough spot in December, weighing another rate hike but concerned about the speed with which a larger market correction could ripple through the economy.” Fresh economic PCE readings of hot, sticky, and broadening inflation in October and revised, sharply higher third-quarter GDP at 4.3% — the fastest pace since late 2023 — released Nov. 25 give central bankers ample reasons to lean hawkish with a 25-basis-point rate hike at the Federal Open Market Committee Dec. 8-9. Minutes after those headlines crossed, the Trump administration unveiled proposed new tariffs targeting 14 major trading partners, including China, Japan, and the European Union, to counter what the administration calls foreign “excess industrial capacity.” Truist Advisory Services Head of U.S. Economics Mike Skordeles said the year-over-year increase of headline and core PCE and the revised GDP report further confirm “for us that the Fed will deliver a quarter-point hike in December.’’ Skordeles said in an exclusive email to TheStreet that the proposed tariffs won’t be enacted until January at the earliest and won’t affect specific industries with national security-related levies, such as steel, aluminum and automobiles. “The combination of the factors should limit the near-term implications, especially for most consumers,” Skordeles said. Persistent inflation puts Fed rate hikes in focus The FOMC held rates steady in October at 3.75-4.0% after a 25-basis-point hike in September, amid sticky inflation from tariffs, the Iran War energy shock, and the AI demand-supply dynamic. It was the Fed’s first rate move of the year. Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh vowed before and after taking over the role in May that the price stability side of its dual mandate is the independent central bank’s top commitment now that the labor market has stabilized from its 2025 softness. Four Fed governors — Vice Chair Philip Jefferson, Michael Barr , Lisa Cook and Christopher Waller — and several regional bank presidents recently signaled decidedly hawkish tones, expressing that further policy tightening was necessary to bring inflation back to its 2% target, which it has missed for nearly six years. The Fed made three 25-basis-point cuts at its last three meetings of 2025 due to concerns about the labor market side of its mandate. Those insurance cuts need to be reversed as inflation data shows higher prices not only in energy costs but broadening into other sectors including services, the Fed’s hawks say. So do some Fed watchers. Wall Street banks, including giants J.P. Morgan, Bank of America and Deutsche Bank, are also calling for a 25-basis-point hike in December plus additional 25-basis-point increases in January and March. TheStreet Traders price in Fed rate hikes into 2027 According to the CME Group FedWatch Tool , following the latest inflation readings, futures traders see roughly a 97% to 98% probability of a 25-point-rate hike at the Dec. 8-9 meeting. But it probably won’t be a “one-and-done” deal. CME FedWatch probabilities for the January FOMC meeting point to a strong chance of additional tightening, including a roughly 40.7% probability of another 25-basis-point hike and a 58.4% chance of a cumulative 50-basis-point increase. Markets also price in an additional rate increase in March if policymakers are unable to cool demand. President Donald Trump and his allies have repeatedly called for lower interest rates of 1% or less for years, with the president blasting the Fed’s most recent actions as political retribution. Trump has said the lower rates will help the depressed U.S. housing market plus reduce the interest the government pays on its $40.71 trillion debt. New tariffs aim to boost, balance American trade U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer’s office unveiled the proposals following an eight-month investigation into foreign industrial overcapacity and set the maximum potential tariff rates of 20% to 40%. Separately, the administration proposed a new 10% tariff on finished commercial aircraft from Brazil and higher duties on over-quota Brazilian sugar after talks with the South American nation stalled. The new tariff push, while not viewed as sweeping as April’s Liberation Day announcement, lands just three weeks after midterm elections reflected voter frustration over higher costs of living and skepticism about Wall Street, where volatility has been fueled by AI and other tech jitters. Dean Lyulkin, the CEO of Cardiff, a San Diego-based small business lender, said the Trump administration’s proposed tariffs fall mainly on Vietnam and Southeast Asia, and mostly on furniture, clothing and other consumer goods. Related: Fed faces a dangerous inflation dilemma as recession fears grow “Even there, the additional tariff applies to the wholesale import value, not the retail price, and amounts to just 5% to 10% more,’’ Lyulkin said in an exclusive email to TheStreet. Critics warn that new import levies amount to a tax on consumers and risk triggering another round of price increases that could force the Fed to keep interest rates higher for longer. “There is zero reason for anyone, including investors and small business owners, to panic,’’ Lyulkin said. “If this headline is used to explain the market correction happening now, or to suggest it adds new risks to the U.S. economy, that line of thinking can be quickly dismissed as nonsense.” Fed struggles to lower inflation to 2% target For households carrying credit-card balances, private student loans or adjustable-rate debt, each 25-basis-point hike adds up—and analysts warn that sustained rate hikes could lift Treasury yields and keep borrowing costs elevated well into mid-2027. “The challenge for the Fed is that we need to see 0.2% or less monthly core PCE gains consistently to return inflation to its 2% target,’’ Swonk said, describing the last nearly six years of price pressures as “the longest and most corrosive bout of inflation since the 1970s.” “A fall in pump prices and more promotions among retailers could get us there in November – but it may not stay there,’’ Swonk said. title: Scott Bessent sends the Fed a stern warning it cannot ignore
summary: Scott Bessent stepped into the Fed's most contentious debate of the year. The timing was not an accident.
content: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent stepped into the Federal Reserve’s December debate on Sunday with a warning that the central bank risks over-tightening. Speaking on CBS News ‘ “Face the Nation,” he said financial conditions had already tightened sharply and that piling on another big rate hike could make things worse. The remarks come as stocks slide and the Fed’s next decision draws closer, and the timing matters. The Fed meets on Dec. 8 and 9, and some officials are no longer debating whether to raise rates but how much. Fed Governor Christopher Waller has said a half-point hike “should be considered at the December meeting.” Bessent’s warning lands right in the middle of that fight. Also read: Scott Bessent sends a strong verdict to Nvidia’s stock investors His comments follow a rough stretch for markets. The Nasdaq Composite set a record on Oct. 6 and has since slid deep enough to turn negative for the year. Nvidia alone has lost about $1.7 trillion in market value since its October peak. Scott Bessent puts the Fed on notice on CBS Margaret Brennan asked Bessent how he understood the past week in markets. He said it was “a combination of things,” pointing to “very hawkish remarks from the Federal Reserve” and “a substantial tightening in financial conditions over the past few months,” according to CBS News. Brennan noted that markets had seen “a real sell-off over the past week.” He did not name any Fed official in the interview or say what decision he wants in December. Bessent also used the interview to calm nerves about the financial system. Asked whether Americans should worry about their banks, he said, “They shouldn’t.” Calling them “by far the most resilient companies in the U.S. economy.” His concern, in other words, is the Fed’s next step rather than the plumbing. His tone has shifted in recent weeks. On Oct. 28, Bessent said further rate hikes would not necessarily be a policy mistake and that the December call belonged to the Fed, as reported by CNBC. He also praised Fed Chair Kevin Warsh at the time, saying Warsh was “off to a great start.” He added that he had “great confidence” in the new chair. Polls, AI and a market in retreat Scott Bessent tied part of the sell-off to politics. “The market sell-off actually began as the Democrats moved ahead in the polls and then accelerated after Election Day,” he said. The worst damage came quickly. Two days after the election, the Nasdaq fell 5.52% and the S&P 500 dropped 4.36% as investors weighed the risk of tighter AI regulation. President Donald Trump blamed the Democratic sweep for the slide in a post on Truth Social. “The obvious catalyst for the sharp selloff is that markets are pricing in the midterm results,” eToro analyst Jakub Rochlitz said. Bessent also pointed to AI policy. “The Democratic position on the SI buildout has spooked a lot of investors in terms of slowing it down,” he said. Wedbush analyst Dan Ives called the week a “perfect storm” for tech stocks, citing fears of heavier oversight of AI and data centers under a Democratic Congress. The AI boom cuts both ways for the Fed, though. Richmond Fed President Thomas Barkin has said AI infrastructure spending is adding to near-term inflation through strong demand. “The path of AI feels particularly consequential,” he said in prepared remarks on Nov. 9. Bessent is not telling the Fed what to do, at least not in those words. But the message from Sunday is clear enough. Bloomberg / Getty Images Bessent’s CNBC case against a bigger hike Sunday’s warning built on two earlier CNBC interviews. On Nov. 13, Bessent said “the Fed should understand that this is an energy supply shock,” tied to the conflict with Iran, according to CNBC. He argued that hiking too much into a shock that is already easing would be a mistake, calling the latest inflation readings “very noisy numbers.” “The Fed’s supposed to look into the future, not look in the rearview mirror,” he added. The hawks see it differently. Waller made his case for a bigger move in London, saying a 25-basis-point hike could put the Fed’s credibility at risk. October consumer prices rose 0.4%, above forecasts, lending more weight to his argument. Bessent went back on CNBC on Nov. 20 and urged the Fed not to embrace a big rate hike. He noted that one governor now backing a 50-basis-point hike had wanted a cut of similar size within the past year. “So I would encourage the Fed to look forward, not backwards,” he said. More Federal Reserve: Scott Bessent just reframed the case for a December rate hike Fed Chair Kevin Warsh reveals October surprise inside interest-rate pause How a Fed interest rate pause would impact Main Street investors Wall Street isn’t fully on his side. Bank of America still expects a quarter-point hike in December, but its economists say the risk of a half-point move “has increased substantially.” The bank went further, writing that the Fed’s October hold “is looking like a policy mistake.” JPMorgan expects the Fed to raise rates in December and has penciled in two further hikes in early 2027. Where the Fed stands before December The Fed raised rates by a quarter point in September to a target range of 3.75% to 4%, then paused in October on a 10-2 vote. Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack and Board of Governors member Lisa Cook dissented in favor of a hike. Hammack has said the Fed needs at least two more quarter-point increases. The dissents are part of a broader shift inside the committee. As JPMorgan’s Michele has noted, the internal migration is toward tightening rather than away from it, making the December meeting harder to call than the market is pricing in. The CME FedWatch tool puts the probability of at least a quarter-point hike above 85%. Bessent is not telling the Fed what to do, at least not in those words. But the message from Sunday is clear enough. He sees the recent sell-off as a warning and wants policymakers to weigh the full picture before making a decision. title: Bank of America issues blunt 2027 hard-landing warning on S&P 500
summary: Wall Street may be missing a bigger threat.
content: Judging from Wall Street’s early 2027 stock market forecasts, it might seem that autumn’s turbulence was more or less a brief speed bump. Major investment banks still continue to project another banner year ahead, even after Federal Reserve rate-hike jitters and AI spending doubts knocked the S&P 500 down from its Oct. 6 record of 7,818.93 to 7,201.09 on Nov. 24 . Bank of America Securities isn’t buying that complacency though. In a note shared with me, Chief Investment Strategist Michael Hartnett issued a blunt reality check for investors heading into 2027. Though most on Wall Street are calling for smooth sailing, Hartnett warns that a painful economic slowdown is perhaps the single biggest underpriced risk in markets today and is advising clients to play defense now. Bank of America outlines a possible S&P 500 decline amid recession risks. Spencer Platt / Getty Images Inside Bank of America’s 2027 S&P 500 forecast and hard-landing math Hartnett’s alarm starts off with a growing gap between market nerves and institutional positioning. As per Bank of America’s November Global Fund Manager Survey as reported by Biggo , just 3% of fund managers are forecasting a steep downturn over the next 12 months, in comparison with 50% expecting a soft landing and 42% predicting no landing at all. More Wall Street: Arista Networks stock gets fresh backing from Jim Cramer and Wall Street Oracle stock sinks as Wall Street confronts a $20 billion AI problem Wall Street just got a candid look at who is winning the AI race Cash levels have dropped to a historically thin 3.6%, down from 3.9% in October, even as global stock funds absorbed $310 billion over the past four weeks. That crowding leaves stocks remarkably exposed. Hartnett warned that a “ hard landing ” is the biggest threat to market consensus, arguing that Wall Street projections of 15% to 20% global earnings growth are currently looking too optimistic as AI capital spending and K-shaped wealth effects taper off. In a true bust, he projects a bear market that drags the S&P 500 down to nearly 6,666, implying a 7.4% to 8% downside from late-November levels. For clarity, recession isn’t Bank of America’s base case. Under a “Goldilocks” soft landing scenario that involves global growth above 3%, dropping inflation, sliding oil prices, and 21 global rate cuts in the back half of 2027, Hartnett expects a bull market to broaden out that could potentially carry the S&P 500 to around 7,777, an 8% increase from Nov. 24, yielding 4% to 8% upside for global stocks, with an extreme AI-boom surprise reaching 8,888. That discipline echoes Bank of America’s broader view. In September, BofA U.S. equity chief Savita Subramanian bumped the bank’s 2026 year-end S&P 500 target from 7,100 to 7,400 , along with a 12-month target of 7,800, which is a lot more conservative than the 8,700 targets at Goldman Sachs, Morgan Stanley, and Barclays, or UBS’s 8,900 call. The AI cash crunch, and BofA’s ‘GRAB’ shield before a spring pivot Bank of America is clearly conservative and bracing for significant volatility, while rivals forecast S&P 500 year-end targets of 8,700+. To explain that, it’s important to look at the balance sheets powering AI. BofA projects a whopping $1.3 trillion in AI CapEx in 2027, even with hyperscalers’ free cash flow swinging to a negative $283 billion. That leaves stocks remarkably vulnerable to any spending cut or credit shock. In BofA’s November survey, 52% of fund managers said they expect an AI hyperscaler to announce a CapEx reduction within six months, up from 30% in October, while 34% flagged an AI bubble and 31% cited an AI credit event as top tail risks. Hartnett also mapped out concrete stress lines to watch. This includes an S&P 500 break below its 6,845 year-end 2025 close, initial jobless claims topping 250,000, or investment-grade credit spreads growing beyond 100 basis points. Until investor fear becomes a lot more visible, Hartnett advises hedging with “GRAB” assets. Government bonds: TLT, IEF, and SHY for stability. Real estate: XLRE, offering diversification away from AI. High-quality stocks: AAA-rated companies for defensive exposure. Gold: GLD, potentially benefiting from a weaker dollar. Later opportunities: After rate hikes end, pivot toward semiconductors (SMH), commodities (DBC), Bitcoin (IBIT), and consumer staples (XLP). What Bank of America’s 2027 warning means for investors Hartnett’s playbook is essentially a practical roadmap for sequencing portfolio risk over the next six months. First, it would be wise to look at Bank of America’s three macro green lights before chasing a sustained bull run. This includes the 10-year Treasury yield slipping below 4.5%, WTI crude falling below $70 a barrel, and a clear peak in the U.S. dollar. Until all that aligns, expect choppy trading and stay selective. Second, it’s important for investors to apply the “GRAB” framework to stress-test their allocation. If mega-cap tech and AI names dominate your 401(k) or brokerage account, pairing core stocks with short-to-intermediate Treasuries, AAA-rated quality businesses, or modest real estate and gold exposure cushions a slide toward 6,666. Finally, keep dry powder ready for spring. If interest-rate hikes wrap up in the first half of 2027 without a credit breakdown, beaten-down consumer staples and cyclical sectors might end up offering a far better risk-reward than today’s crowded trades. title: Kevin O’Leary says 99% of people trying to get rich make one mistake
summary: The “Shark Tank” investor says the real money hides in businesses most founders never brag about.
content: Every other startup pitch promises to be the next TikTok. The investor TV audiences know as Mr. Wonderful would rather own something that smells like dry-cleaning solvent. “Shark Tank” investor Kevin O’Leary says the dream of a viral app that mints a billionaire overnight is the trap that catches nearly everyone trying to get rich fast. His alternative won’t impress anyone at a dinner party, but it pays. Read more: Kevin O’Leary calls this ‘the best side hustle there is’ for turning $0 into $10,000 in 30 days The viral app dream has a customer problem The fantasy he keeps hearing, especially from students and young founders, goes something like this. Build an app, watch it explode, and become a billionaire in a month. “Never happens,” O’Leary said in a conversation with Tetr College of Business in May. “99% of apps fail because they can’t acquire customers, no matter how good the app is. Just they can’t break through. TikTok kind of thing only happens once in a lifetime… once a decade.” In his telling, the product is rarely what sinks the company. Reaching customers is. A brilliant app that nobody downloads still earns exactly zero. Kevin O’Leary has spent years on “Shark Tank” deciding which businesses are worth backing. Savion Washington / Getty Images Dry cleaners don’t need an algorithm O’Leary would rather back the businesses most founders scroll right past. He prefers “boring” companies, like dry cleaning or insecticide, because they already bring in revenue and free cash flow. “You get very rich very quickly if you’re part of a positive cash flow business and you simply save it, reinvest it,” he said. That same habit, according to O’Leary, is how people build the $5 million in liquid assets, often parked in Treasury bills, that he sees as the threshold for true financial freedom . “That’s how you get your five million in the bank,” he said. Government data leans his way. Of the private-sector businesses that opened in the year ending March 2021, 47.2% were still operating in March 2026, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics . The information sector , which includes software publishers along with media and telecom companies, did worse, at 41.4%. Other services , the category that covers repair shops and dry cleaners, came in at 55.4%. Read more Kevin O’Leary: Kevin O’Leary says he ‘can’t stand it’ when people blow $28 on lunch if they only make $70,000 Kevin O’Leary’s 3 ‘big’ economic predictions for 2027: ‘I’m going out on a limb here’ Kevin O’Leary tells Gen Z security guard working 80 hours a week he’s ‘not looking hard enough’ for better job Chasing a payday is a lousy business plan The app warning fits something O’Leary has said for years. Chasing money for its own sake doesn’t work. “If you’re hungry for money, I guarantee you’ll fail 100%,” O’Leary said on “The Iced Coffee Hour” podcast in May 2024. He thinks the founders who make it focus on solving problems and executing every day. He calls his approach “signal versus noise,” a rule built around three key tasks per day. Venture capital gets the same treatment. Eighty percent of venture-backed deals fail, he said in the Tetr College of Business conversation, mostly because founders ignore what it costs to acquire customers or refuse to admit when an idea isn’t working. The least exciting pitch in the room Nobody has ever gone viral for buying a laundromat. That may be the whole point. O’Leary’s formula has no lottery ticket in it. Find or build a business that throws off cash, then save and reinvest what it earns. The founders betting everything on a once-a-decade breakout are playing far longer odds than the person running the dry cleaner down the street. title: Salesforce wants to get paid per answer, not per worker
summary: Salesforce is rewriting how it bills, and one new product earns nothing unless the bot fixes your problem. Wall Street is watching closely.
content: Type a question into a company’s help chat, and if the bot solves your problem, that business may owe Salesforce a fee. Ask for a human or walk away unhappy, and Salesforce collects nothing. That is how Salesforce prices its Help Agent , a service bot it launched in June. “Your cost is tied to outcomes, not activity,” the company said. The detail may sound small, but it previews how Salesforce (CRM) plans to make money as AI does more of the work. Also read: Salesforce’s biggest risk now is customers who never log in A Bank of America research note shared with TheStreet shows why that matters now. Analyst Tal Liani and his team kept a Buy rating and a $285 target ahead of Salesforce’s Dec. 2 earnings. Yet the bank’s talks with Salesforce’s consulting partners indicate a core business that is adding users only slowly. Fewer workers means fewer seats to sell Salesforce has long charged a monthly fee for each employee who logs in, which works best when customers are hiring. Partners told Bank of America that seat growth is “tepid” as companies weigh whether AI can cut staffing needs. One large partner put Sales Cloud seat growth at zero to 1% in the September quarter, according to the note. Salesforce has already shown how this plays out. CEO Marc Benioff said last year that AI agents let him cut Salesforce’s support staff from 9,000 to about 5,000. “I need less heads,” he told a podcast , and every customer that copies him needs fewer Salesforce logins. Benioff acknowledged the bind on the company’s August earnings call . “We’re still trapped in some ways in old per user pricing models,” he told a Goldman Sachs analyst. His way out is to charge for work the software finishes, not the people using it. Salesforce’s new Help Agent charges businesses only when the bot resolves a customer’s issue on its own, a break from billing for every user who logs in. Gary Hershorn / Getty Images Charging per answer is harder than it sounds The catch is that seats are easy to budget and answers are not. Nobody knows in advance how many questions an AI agent will field. That uncertainty is showing up in deals. One large partner said customers’ most basic question is “how many Flex credits would I consume,” the units Salesforce uses to meter AI work. At that partner, Agentforce pilots have slipped to about a fifth of customers from a peak near a third, with little progress toward paid use. Salesforce hears the same caution. President and COO Miguel Milano told analysts in August that one large customer wanted to try it to see the value before buying upfront. Salesforce is now negotiating a possible outcome-based deal with it. Per-answer pricing also ties revenue to how often the bots succeed. Salesforce said in June that its own help site resolved 70% of inquiries, but by August it cited 64% of more than 5 million conversations. Under this model, every chat the bot can’t close earns nothing. Answers also cost money to deliver. Bank of America expects operating margin to shrink about 1.1 percentage points from a year earlier in the October quarter, mostly from higher AI consumption costs. A sold seat costs little to serve, but every answer burns computing power. Salesforce is buying time with bigger contracts Meanwhile, Salesforce is leaning on familiar levers. Partners told Bank of America that add-on products, regional rollouts and list-price increases are lifting contract values even as seat growth stays weak. Customers are also signing longer contracts in exchange for discounts and setup funding. One midsize partner said at least 70% of its renewals ran three years or more, according to the note. That steadies revenue but delays the day investors learn how many seats AI removes. Salesforce is betting its customers will make the same shift. Its deal for m3ter, the note says, adds usage-based billing to Salesforce’s revenue software, enabling customers to charge their own clients based on consumption or outcomes. Bank of America expects organic growth, which strips out the Informatica acquisition, to climb from 6.4% in the July quarter to 7.4% in the October quarter. That number will show whether the bridge is holding. More Artificial Intelligence: AI investments fail when companies ignore the hard part of transformation Morgan Stanley issues a fresh warning about AI stocks CrowdStrike gives companies a ‘kill switch’ as bots go off script How Bank of America’s call stacks up That matters beyond Salesforce, whose software runs sales and service work at many large companies. Its results test whether seat-based software can adapt to AI. Bank of America thinks the stock’s roughly 27% drop since its Sept. 3 peak has created a positive short-term setup. Its $285 target values the whole business, including debt, at 16 times expected 2027 free cash flow, a modest premium over software peers. Most of Wall Street sees it the same way. Salesforce carries a consensus Buy rating from 56 analysts, and their median target matches Bank of America’s $285, according to Stock Analysis . Not everyone is convinced. Morgan Stanley, UBS, and Wells Fargo kept Hold ratings in late October, with targets between $235 and $260 . BTIG kept its Buy rating on Nov. 18 but cut its target to $250 from $300. Dec. 2 will test both camps, starting with organic growth. Beat Bank of America’s 7.4% forecast, and Salesforce buys time for answers to catch on. Miss it, and higher prices no longer cover slow seat growth, a warning to every rival that bills by the user. title: Goldman Sachs resets Broadcom's 12-month price target before earnings
summary: AVGO AI funding and 2028 data center concerns grow.
content: Earlier this year, in September, before fiscal Q3 2026 earnings, I wrote about Morgan Stanley warning that Broadcom’s biggest risk going into earnings was expectations, not fundamentals. That framing has aged well. Broadcom (AVGO) hit an all-time intraday high of $495 on June 3, 2026 (the day after Q3 results). On Nov. 25, it hit a 52-week low of $278 and was down over 19% intraday. In a note shared with me at TheStreet, Goldman Sachs weighed in, trying to explain how a company growing this fast ended up here. Also Read: Google’s 2027 chip plan is bad news for Broadcom The firm kept its Buy rating but lowered its 12-month price target to $460 from $540 (a 15% decline, according to the note). Its analysts also said expectations are “muted heading into the print.” So why would a firm that still likes the stock cut its target by nearly 15%? Why Goldman cut Broadcom’s target but kept the Buy The answer is the multiple, not the business. Goldman now applies a 25x multiple to its normalized earnings per share (EPS) estimate of $18.00, down from 30x, according to the note. The EPS estimate itself did not change. The firm cited lower multiples across peer stocks. My own math puts 25 times $18 at $450, so the stated $460 target likely reflects rounding. Either way, the lesson is the same. The whole sector got cheaper, and Broadcom came down with it. That takes me back to a Jim Cramer comment in a piece I covered: “If there is going to be a turn, the stock of Broadcom will let you know.” More Broadcom: Broadcom CEO says capital is ‘available’ after banks wavered Jim Cramer praises Broadcom and recommends buying another iconic stock Broadcom fought AT&T over VMware: Now a telecom giant is all in The stock was $341.60 when Goldman published on Nov. 17, implying 35% upside, according to the note. Since then, it has slid to roughly $301. At that price, the $460 target implies 53% upside, based on my calculation. Goldman also expects modest upside to results and guidance when Broadcom reports on Dec. 9 after the market closes. Its fiscal 2027 and 2028 AI revenue estimates sit 5% and 9% above Wall Street consensus, with EPS estimates 5% and 12% higher, according to the note. The three questions Goldman says will move Broadcom Goldman does not think the quarter itself will decide this. It thinks three answers will. First is incremental details on FY27 AI guidance. Emerging hyperscalers account for about 6.3 gigawatts of Broadcom’s roughly 10 gigawatts of custom chip deployments that year, according to the note. Many of those customers depend on outside funding. Goldman said any added visibility there “could be impactful.” Related: Jim Cramer praises Broadcom and recommends buying another iconic stock Second is customer readiness in fiscal 2028. Emerging hyperscalers represent about 75% of Broadcom’s planned 20-gigawatt target. Since the midterm elections, investors have scrutinized whether land, power, and building shells will actually be available. Think of it as a simple question. Can customers build the data centers that Broadcom’s chips are meant to fill? Third is competition. Goldman wants more detail on the durability of Broadcom’s relationship with Google as rivals such as MediaTek gain ground, according to the note. CEO Hock Tan has pointed to the same physical limits. On the September earnings call , he called building an AI data center a “multidimensional problem” involving land, power, and shell. Goldman is taking him at his word. Anthropic is expected to become Broadcom’s largest custom chip customer in 2027, with line of sight to 10 gigawatts by 2028. Bloomberg / Getty Images What Broadcom has already promised The bull case rests on numbers Broadcom has already put in writing. Fiscal third-quarter revenue was $29.6 billion, up 86% year-over-year (YoY). AI semiconductor revenue reached $16.7 billion, up 221% YoY. Free cash flow was $13.7 billion, or 46% of revenue. Management guided fiscal fourth-quarter revenue to about $34.8 billion, up 93%, with AI revenue of $21.7 billion. Beyond that, Tan laid out AI revenue of $115 billion in fiscal 2027 and $230 billion in fiscal 2028, which he said is based on secured supply, according to the earnings call transcript . Related: Jim Cramer now sees a buying opportunity in beaten-down space stock Customers are named. Anthropic is expected to become Broadcom’s largest custom chip customer in 2027, with line of sight to 10 gigawatts by 2028. OpenAI has a 1.3 gigawatt plan for 2027. Broadcom also began shipping Google’s next-generation TPU version 8i. There is one soft spot. Gross margin fell to 75% in the third quarter, down 210 basis points from the prior quarter, and is guided to about 73% in the fourth, according to CFO Amie Thuener . She said memory-heavy chips are “diluting” margins. That is the cost of selling more complete systems. What I make of this setup I find it hard to call this a broken story. It looks more like a stock that grew into a valuation too quickly. Broadcom is down 18.66% year-to-date and 26.88% over the past year, as of intraday Nov. 25. The three-year return is still 217.73%. If you hold an S&P 500 index fund, you own a slice of this. So the swings reach well beyond traders. I think the funding question is the right one to focus on. A $230 billion target is only as good as the checks that fund it, and Goldman is asking for exactly that. Still, the firm says it expects Broadcom to beat modestly. Low expectations plus a decent report is how stocks recover. So, on Dec. 9, Tan will either allay funding concerns or confirm them. title: BofA resets Dell stock price target by $100 after record earnings
summary: BofA cuts its DELL price target despite a record $54.9 billion quarter, questioning AI growth sustainability.
content: I’ve learned that a stock can deliver impressive results and still struggle to move higher. Sometimes, the market is less interested in what a company has just achieved than in whether it can keep delivering at the same pace. Dell Technologies (DELL) reported a record third quarter on Nov. 24, raised guidance, and still fell about 5% in early trading the following day. Seven of the eight firms that updated price targets lowered them, according to TheFly . Bank of America’s Wamsi Mohan, ranked 26th out of 12,606 analysts on TipRanks with a 59% success rate, cut his target to $500 from $600 in a note shared with TheStreet, a 16.67% reduction. His reasoning? “The market continues to question sustainability.” DELL is still up 129.34% year to date and 129.27% over one year as of Nov. 25, according to Yahoo Finance . This is despite recording an all-time high of $595.51 on Sept. 18, 2026, and currently trading 52% below the high. The stock is not struggling. The question is how much growth is already in the price. Also Read: Dell Technologies Q3 2027 Earnings: Recap of $DELL Earnings Call, Stock Forecast Dell’s tension: a great quarter, a lower multiple Mohan said Dell delivered another strong quarter and outlook. What he changed was the valuation multiple he applies to Dell’s earnings, citing risks to the AI infrastructure buildout and Dell’s exposure to neoclouds. These newer AI-focused cloud providers have leaned heavily on debt to expand. That worry has a backdrop. Piper Sandler pointed to the “sharp sell-off across AI and infrastructure names over the last two months, according to Stocktwits .” More Tech: Apple CEO signals surprising change for iPhone users Comcast sends wake-up call to employees as customers cut services AI agents’ growing role in payments raises an awkward question I covered the same fear when Oracle ‘s credit spreads widened, and its bonds were questioned. The debate has moved from whether AI demand is real to who is financing it, and for how long. Dell’s answer came from COO Jeff Clarke on the earnings call: “We’ve had no customers reschedule business. The backlog continues to be very firm.” He said the company remains “highly selective” with Neocloud customers and that every order is “rigorously vetted for customer quality and access to capital, land and power.” What the Dell quarter showed According to Dell’s earnings release , Q3 revenue was a record $54.9 billion, up 103%. Non-GAAP EPS was $9.45, up 265%. Cash flow from operations was a record $4.5 billion for a third quarter. The Infrastructure Solutions Group did the heavy lifting: $42 billion in revenue, up 198%, with operating income of $7.1 billion and a margin up 460 basis points to 17%. AI server revenue was $22 billion, up 291%. Related: Trump’s 5 words helped drive a massive 350% rally so what’s next? Dell booked $60.2 billion in new AI orders, the second straight quarter above $60 billion, according to the Q3 earnings call transcript , and ended with a record $132.3 billion backlog. I covered the $95 billion backlog in September and the President Donald Trump “buy a Dell” story, and the backlog has grown by $37 billion since. Guidance moved up. Full-year revenue is now $202 billion, up 78%, with AI server revenue of $78 billion. Q4 revenue is guided to $56.25 billion at the midpoint, up 69%. The Dell detail the analysts keep pointing to The beat did not come only from AI servers. Piper Sandler and Goldman Sachs said traditional servers drove it. Traditional servers and networking revenue was $15 billion, up 235%, as companies upgrade old equipment and add capacity for inference. Clarke said the installed base of traditional servers is older than ever, and software can’t meet new security and performance requirements. That matters because it broadens the story. Demand is not coming only from neoclouds. Raymond James’ Simon Leopold noted margins expanded despite a heavier mix of lower-margin AI hardware, which he reads as operating leverage. Non-GAAP operating expenses fell to 7% of revenue, the lowest in the company’s 42-year history. Related: Goldman Sachs resets Palantir Stock 12-month price target by 18% Even the cautious firms stayed positive. Bernstein’s Mark Newman called the quarter “exceptionally strong” and named Dell his top AI infrastructure pick, though he cut his target to $580 from $650, according to Investing.com . Raymond James and Wells Fargo cited the backlog as support for fiscal 2028, and Piper Sandler expects demand to stay ahead of supply into 2027. The weak spot is PCs. Client Solutions revenue rose just 3% to $12.9 billion, and operating income fell 6%, as customers deferred refreshes to prioritize servers and storage. Dell’s Q3 revenue was a record $54.9 billion, up 103%. Panama7 / Getty Images What to watch Clarke flagged a supply risk: “The gap between component supply and end-user demand continues to widen.” Strong demand helps only if Dell can ship. According to the Q3 earnings call transcript , Dell returned a record $4.9 billion to shareholders, repurchased 9 million shares at an average of $488, and added a $25 billion repurchase authorization. Buying back stock near $488 says management thinks the price is fair. My read is that the target cuts are about the multiple, not the business. The risk is that a lower multiple cannot withstand any wobbles in Neocloud financing or component supply. The next test is the Q4 report, with AI server revenue guided to $23.5 billion. title: Goldman Sachs sends strong signal on Amazon stock before Black Friday
summary: One overlooked detail could change the entire outlook.
content: Every Black Friday, my online shopping routine follows the same script. I tell myself I’m grabbing just a few gifts, but by the time the cardboard boxes stack up by the front door, half my cart is filled with everyday basics, including coffee pods, paper towels, and laundry detergent, tossed in because one-click next-day shipping makes it all effortless. If your own Amazon ( AMZN ) cart resembles mine, you are witnessing firsthand what has Goldman Sachs analysts leaning in hard. Just days ahead of official Black Friday shopping and Amazon’s flagship cloud conference , in a note shared with me, Goldman Sachs just delivered a high-conviction signal on Amazon stock. As nervous traders continue to punish Big Tech over hefty spending bills, Goldman argues the market is misreading two powerful profit engines hiding in plain sight. Inside Goldman Sachs’ $370 retail thesis for Amazon stock Goldman Sachs analyst Eric Sheridan and his team reiterated a Buy rating on Amazon, keeping its stock on the firm’s Americas Conviction List, and reiterating its $370 12-month price target. That call implies around a 46.7% upside from Amazon stock’s November 24 finish at $252.29. Sheridan didn’t mince words about the setup, stating that Amazon’s pricing setup “…leaves the stock as the most compelling risk/reward in our mega/large cap coverage from current levels.” Read more: Amazon, Walmart, and Target’s holiday returns hide a catch A core pillar of that call stems from changes in everyday shopping habits. According to the bank, instead of losing shoppers to outside chatbots, Amazon’s first-party AI assistant, Alexa for Shopping, generated around $12 billion in incremental sales across over 300 million users in 2025. It is projected to climb 33% year over year to $16 billion or more across 400 million users in 2026. Shoppers using it convert at 16%, a 60% lift over the 10% e-commerce baseline, while new “Shop Direct” and “Buy for Me” features allow Amazon to complete purchases even on external brand sites. Meanwhile, fresh grocery and Everyday Essentials grew at about three times the rate of other categories and now account for 50% of all U.S. units sold. That’s backed up by a brand new Uber Eats Prime perk across 10,000 cities and a high-frequency “halo effect” in which active grocery shoppers spend over twice as much across non-grocery categories. Lower-priced staples ended up compressing Q3 stores contribution profit by around 220 basis points, but Goldman argues investors are overlooking automation. Amazon is now running more than 1 million fulfillment robots , potentially cutting per-unit cost-to-serve by around 13% by 2030, from $6.38 to $5.50. Goldman Sachs reiterates its Buy rating and $370 price target on Amazon. Bloomberg / Getty Images The $578 billion AWS catalyst heading into re:Invent Black Friday checkout traffic is just one part of the story. Amazon will host AWS re:Invent in Las Vegas, running from Nov. 30 through Dec. 4, putting its cloud division back in focus. Sheridan’s team believes Wall Street remains behind the curve on cloud acceleration, writing that “we are in the early innings of an AWS estimate revision cycle that remains underappreciated by investors.” After AWS grew 39% year over year in Q3 , management forecast 40% or higher annualized growth in both 2027 and 2028, while outlining a path to a $1 trillion cloud business within five to 10 years. More Amazon: Amazon cuts more jobs as CEO touts record margins, retail gains Amazon’s latest report left stock investors with one big question Amazon’s $75 AI wearable hides a bigger $144-a-year bet The underlying AI momentum is remarkable. Amazon’s annualized AWS AI revenue run rate jumped from more than $15 billion in the first quarter to more than $25 billion in the second quarter. Goldman forecasts AI services surging from $28.1 billion (15.9% of AWS revenue) in 2026 to $136.9 billion (40.7%) by 2028, while keeping consolidated AWS margins durable in the high-30s, backed by a year-end backlog that skyrockets 136.9% to $578 billion. As AWS grows its Bedrock AI platform for businesses and prepares to sell its custom Trainium chips to outside customers by late 2027, Goldman Sachs points to substantial growth potential. In fact, in its most optimistic scenario, the bank estimates AWS cloud revenue could potentially rise by 54% to 55% over the next two years. What Goldman’s signal means for Amazon stock investors Despite near-unanimous Wall Street backing, with consensus targets ranging from $326 to $331, investor mood around Amazon has remained cautious. Yet that skepticism has opened a rare valuation window. Amazon trades near 23.5 times forward earnings , a 58% discount to its 10-year median of 56.5 times, roughly aligning with Microsoft’s mid-20s multiple and far below Apple’s 33-plus multiple , and just 17.4 times Goldman’s 2028 earnings estimate. Goldman Sachs estimates that the stock could potentially drop to $190 in a worst-case scenario or climb to $500 if things go well, underscoring a wide range of possible outcomes for investors. For long-term investors, the playbook is clear. It’s important to monitor Black Friday order volumes and AWS CEO Matt Garman’s Dec. 1 re:Invent keynote for updates on Trainium adoption and Bedrock demand. Instead of chasing post-event spikes, using pre-holiday pullbacks to build positions in stages allows for capturing both Amazon’s everyday shopping dominance and its accelerating cloud cycle. title: Home Depot shoppers can now dodge a classic cart disaster
summary: The retailer's AI tool now performs an action that shoppers could be thankful for.
content: If you’ve ever driven to the nearest Home Depot to grab parts you think you need, only to realize halfway through the job that something doesn’t fit, Home Depot (HD) has something for you. The company has given its AI assistant, called Magic Apron , a big upgrade. The tool can now scan an image of your shopping cart for compatible parts before you reach the register, Business Insider reported. That way, you can spot the wrong parts before leaving the store, which saves you a return trip. How Magic Apron catches mistakes before you leave the store To run the check, you simply open the Home Depot app in the store, snap a photo of your cart, and ask the AI to review whether everything in it is compatible with the project you are working on. If a part is missing from your cart or you picked the wrong item, the tool flags it right away. Also read: 3 under-the-radar picks Wall Street’s sharpest minds like now According to a report by Business Insider , Rebecca Godecke, the senior vice president of Home Depot’s online division, gave an example of a shopper picking up supplies to replace a toilet in an interview. After the shopper took a picture of the cart for the AI, it flagged an incompatible item among them. “Magic Apron was able to identify that and say, ‘You have an incompatible wax ring. You need to go back to this aisle and try again,'” Godecke said. That alert saved the customer from a leaky bathroom and a return trip. Magic Apron now works in all 2,000-plus U.S. Home Depot stores, and the AI tool works in multiple languages. Home Depot shoppers may dodge a classic cart disaster as the retailer’s AI tool can now check a picture of your shopping cart to catch wrong parts before you leave the store. P_Wei / Getty Images Why this matters for Home Depot’s business Home Depot mostly makes money by selling tools, lumber, appliances, and services to DIY customers and professional contractors. For a company like that, wrong purchases can really hurt the business. Items returned by customers cost money to process, and shoppers who give up on projects tend to stop coming back. That’s why this upgrade is important for Home Depot. Also, Fortune reported that mortgage rates are hovering near 7%. That could lead to fewer Americans moving. When fewer people move, it tends to affect Home Depot’s business. That’s why the AI tool upgrades came at a good time. With the upgrade, Home Depot can ensure everyday repair and maintenance shoppers keep coming back. What Home Depot’s latest earnings show Home Depot reported its third-quarter fiscal 2026 results on November 17. The company posted $43.4 billion in revenue, up 4.9% from a year earlier. Its adjusted earnings also came in at $3.86 per share, and its comparable sales rose 2.2%. In the same release, Home Depot named Richard McPhail as its new CEO, effective November 23, Benzinga reported. Ted Decker stepped down as president and CEO but will stay on as chairman of the board. Meanwhile, Ann-Marie Campbell became president and COO, and Jordan Broggi took over as the new CFO, according to Home Depot’s SEC filing. How other retailers are responding Home Depot is not the only chain with an AI tool that helps shoppers. Some other retailers have their own AI assistants. Lowe’s has Mylow, Walmart uses Sparky, Target has Ask Target, and Amazon offers Rufus. What sets Magic Apron apart from most of these tools is its focus on completing full home projects. The tool guides shoppers through every step, from picking the right parts to finishing the installation. In my view, that project-first approach is an advantage for Home Depot, since most shoppers walk in with a specific task they want to finish. title: Jim Cramer sends strong words to stock market investors
summary: Jim Cramer believes Wall Street is refusing to call this market what it is.
content: Most investors check the S&P 500, see a correction, and assume the damage is spread evenly. It isn’t. The market has shed roughly $8 trillion since its Oct. 6 peak, but the pain has landed in uneven bursts that can hit one portfolio even harder than the next. That is what makes a rolling bear so tricky. By the time a sector’s slide makes the headlines, the selling has often moved somewhere else. As Jim Cramer pointed out on a Nov. 17 episode of “Mad Money,” “Everyone seems to be reluctant to call this market what it really is: a rolling bear market that’s ripping off the faces of everybody,” he said. “It’s a rotating bear of a market. It mauls the industrials, then goes after the software stocks, then it hits the hardware, heads for the financials, finds the transports, crushes housing. Sectors can run, but they just can’t hide,” as reported by 247 Wall St. Where the bear has already bitten Look under the hood and it gets uglier. Ron Insana estimates that somewhere between 40% and 50% of S&P 500 companies have fallen at least 20% since market momentum peaked in June. The index itself held up far better than that, which is why so many people are surprised when they open their statements. Also read: Jim Cramer sees something Wall Street may be missing in Broadcom Tech has taken the most visible beating. The Nasdaq-100 sank 5.6% on Nov. 20 and came close to bear market territory, as reported by Yahoo Finance. Chipmakers that carried the AI rally suddenly became the stocks everyone wanted to dump first, and the selling spilled into names with little direct AI exposure. Housing tells a quieter but equally grim story. Builder confidence fell to 25 in November, its lowest level since April 2012, the National Association of Home Builders reported. Nearly half of builders cut prices, and the group’s chief economist said mortgage rates above 7% are holding buyers back. Nvidia is a good example of how fast the mood can swing. The stock jumped 31.48% on Nov. 23 after Jensen Huang was brought back as CEO. Even after that pop, many holders were still underwater after weeks of sharp declines. Let your mix do the heavy lifting Jim Cramer says sectors can run but can’t hide. That is a pretty good argument against betting everything on one corner of the market. Earlier this year, Vanguard floated the idea that a portfolio with 40% in stocks and 60% in bonds could earn about the same as a classic 60/40 split with less risk. The firm calls it a concept, not a mandate. That doesn’t mean flipping an allocation overnight. An investor who is sitting at 80% stocks and 20% bonds might only need a modest shift to 70/30, Moneywise reported. Age, goals, and time horizon should drive that decision. And not the latest selloff or the loudest voice on TV. Rebalancing is the most unglamorous part. Insana has said that investors whose S&P 500 index funds have outpaced their individual stocks should consider trimming that index exposure. He treats it as routine housekeeping rather than a bet on where the market goes next. Taking a little off the winners and topping up the laggards keeps a portfolio from drifting into more risk than you signed up for. It also helps to sort money by purpose. Insana recommends separating long-term retirement savings from near-term expenses and tactical cash. And keeping money for something like a down payment out of stocks entirely, as reported by TheStreet. That way a rolling bear can’t wreck a plan with a short deadline. Jim Cramer says sectors can run but can’t hide. That is a pretty good argument against betting everything on one corner of the market. Spencer Platt / Getty Images Let bonds and cash carry more weight Bonds, at least, are paying again. The 10-year Treasury yield jumped 14 basis points to 5% on Nov. 10 after October consumer prices rose more than forecast. By Nov. 13, traders viewed a December rate hike as certain, as reported by TheStreet. That stings borrowers, but anyone buying bonds now locks in a far higher yield than they could have a few years ago. Savers have options too. The Treasury raised the composite rate on Series I savings bonds to 5.51%, which is the highest since May 2023. Purchases are capped at $10,000 per person each year, and the bonds can’t be cashed in during the first year. For money that can sit untouched for a while, that is a solid deal. High-yield savings accounts also look far better than the bank average. The top accounts offered around 4.40% APY in mid-November, while the national savings average sat at just 0.57%, according to Bankrate. Leaving emergency cash in a low-paying account is a quiet way to lose ground to inflation. Insana suggests parking temporary cash in three- and six-month Treasury bills until markets settle. He also dismissed bitcoin as a safe haven, since it failed to hold up when stocks started sliding. What investors should know Selling after a big drop can turn a temporary loss into a permanent one. Missing just the five best days in the market from 1988 through 2023 would have cut a hypothetical portfolio’s value by as much as 37%, according to 247 Wall St. Many of those best days tend to show up right when fear is at its peak. Nov. 23 showed how quickly that can happen. Nvidia shares soared more than 30%, and both the Nasdaq and the S&P 500 had their best session since April 2025. Anyone who sold in the Nov. 20 rout watched the whole rally from the sidelines. History offers some comfort for patient investors. Bull markets have erased every prior correction and bear market in the S&P 500’s history. Cramer may be right that this bear keeps rolling, but a steady plan and a balanced mix give investors a far better shot at riding it out. title: Medicare open enrollment ends Dec. 7: Last-minute checks for Medicare Advantage, Part D, and Medigap
summary: Surging 2027 drug costs, canceled Medicare Advantage plans, and 15% to 30% Medigap rate hikes require immediate action before Dec. 7.
content: Medicare’s annual election period ends Dec. 7 , and the Thanksgiving holiday leaves even fewer working days than the calendar shows. I interviewed Jae Oh, author of “Maximize Your Medicare,” who said this year’s drug costs could be reason enough for some people to change Medicare Advantage plans. People in a Medicare Advantage plan that has been canceled have a rare chance to move to Medigap without medical underwriting, he added. And for anyone who believes Medigap premiums rise by a predictable 5% to 7% a year, Oh said that assumption no longer holds. Below is a transcript of my interview with Oh, edited for brevity and clarity. When does Medicare’s annual election period end? Bob Powell: Medicare’s annual election period ends Dec. 7. The clock is ticking. Jae Oh: It is. Dec. 7 is just a few days away, and Thanksgiving falls in between. That really cuts down the number of days you effectively have left. What happens if you do nothing with Medicare Advantage? Powell: Let’s start with people who have a Medicare Advantage plan. What should they be thinking about? Oh: First, if you do nothing, your existing plan will automatically renew. What if your Medicare Advantage plan was canceled? Oh: Second, if your plan has been canceled where you live, you actually have more time than Dec. 7. You’re covered through the end of the year, and you get a special enrollment period. It lets you choose another Medicare Advantage plan for January, and it also gives you a special enrollment period into Medigap. It’s one of the unintended consequences of plans leaving an area or being canceled: You get this right without medical underwriting. Say you chose a Medicare Advantage plan years ago and have had buyer’s remorse since. This is your window to make that change. Can you switch from Medicare Advantage to Medigap? Powell: People whose plans weren’t canceled may also be able to switch from Medicare Advantage to Medigap, but they may face underwriting. Oh: That’s certainly the case, and with time this short, that window is closing even faster. Switching from Medicare Advantage to Medigap is possible. The reason to talk about it now is Part D. Leaving your Medicare Advantage plan is no problem. But you need your Part D drug plan and your Medigap policy in place, so you’re not left in no man’s land without the extra coverage that caps your out-of-pocket health care costs. Can you still change plans after Jan. 1? Powell: People who stay in a Medicare Advantage plan, whether it’s their current one or a new one, get one more chance to change in the first quarter of 2027. Oh: Very few people use this option, but it exists. If, and only if, you’re a member of a Medicare Advantage plan on Jan. 1, you can change once to another Medicare Advantage plan during the first quarter. What should you check before picking a Medicare Advantage plan? Powell: What’s your checklist for choosing a Medicare Advantage plan: doctor networks, drug formularies? Oh: The first spot for me is the network. You’re trying to lower your costs, and the best way to do that is to avoid surprises. Checking the network reduces, as far as you can control it, the chance of a bad surprise when you show your insurance card at the billing counter. Second, our client base nationwide is showing us that stand-alone prescription drug plan costs, and the drug costs inside Medicare Advantage plans, have moved more than in other years. [They’ve moved] enough that it could be reason to change Medicare Advantage plans. That’s our anecdotal evidence. Why should Medigap enrollees reevaluate their plans now? Powell: I don’t usually think of the annual election period as a time to change my Medigap plan. Should people in original Medicare and Medigap reevaluate now? Oh: I think we’ve discussed this before. A growing trend, and it continues, is that Medigap rate increases are very high. The old idea of 5% to 7% a year is no longer valid. We are seeing 15%, 20%, 30%. One takeaway for your audience: I don’t find it a productive use of time to try to outguess the carriers. They weigh many inputs when they set rates. But it’s not complete guesswork. They have to get their rates approved by the state. Should you drop Medigap Plan G to save money? Powell: People often say they’ll get Medigap Plan G because it covers so much. But switching to a plan that covers less may not save much on premiums. Is that fair to say? Oh: It’s complicated. It’s always complicated. For me, the main feature of Plan G is that it covers Part B excess charges, and some states don’t allow Part B providers to charge them at all. You may be unlikely to run into a Part B excess charge, but if you do, the cost is very high, and that creates uncertainty. And 2027 will be yet another year in which Medicare payments to doctors decline in nominal terms. Related: She was ready to retire. Six months later, she still couldn’t let go of work

title: Chick-fil-A will do something in 2026 it only does 2 times a year
summary: Chick-fil-A has revealed its final answer to a major question customers have been wondering about for the 2026 holiday season.
content: For chicken-loving fans nationwide, Chick-fil-A’s weekly Sunday closure is already a tough fact to accept. But with Thanksgiving approaching, customers will have to plan around another day when the popular fast-food chain shuts its doors, leaving fans with fewer opportunities to enjoy its famous chicken sandwiches and waffle fries. Thanksgiving is one of the busiest travel and dining holidays of the year, but many restaurants and retailers temporarily close their locations to give employees time to celebrate with family and friends. Others may operate with reduced hours or remain open, making it important to check business schedules before heading out. Fortunately, Chick-fil-A has confirmed its plans for the upcoming holiday, giving customers time to prepare and arrange their meals ahead of the annual celebration. Is Chick-fil-A closed on Thanksgiving 2026? Here’s some of my previous coverage on Chick-fil-A: Chick-fil-A closes several restaurants Chick-fil-A tests new Chicken & Waffles Sandwiches after popular launch Chick-fil-A closes final experimental restaurant The company recommends ordering ahead and scheduling pickup or delivery before Thanksgiving, as catering menus and availability vary by location . Shutterstock Chick-fil-A’s 2026 holiday menu Although fall hasn’t ended yet, Chick-fil-A has already kicked off its 2026 holiday season with a collection of returning favorites and new menu additions, as well as limited-time merchandise . title: Dessert chain closes nearly all locations after ambitious expansion
summary: The dessert chain keeps closing locations after an ambitious expansion, raising questions about whether its concept can survive as its footprint shrinks.
content: A dessert restaurant chain has quietly closed nearly all its locations less than two years after launching, leaving its once-promising concept with only one remaining restaurant nationwide. The concept brought two popular dessert brands under one roof, aiming to give consumers more options while creating a more efficient restaurant model. However, its rapid contraction raises questions about the concept’s ability to gain traction. Introduced in 2025, Cinnabon Swirl is a dessert restaurant concept that combines Cinnabon and Carvel into a standalone business. The locations are franchised by GoTo Foods, the parent company of Auntie Anne’s, Jamba, McAlister’s Deli, Schlotzsky’s, and Moe’s Southwest Grill. Cinnabon Swirl closes nearly all locations Cinnabon Swirl has closed three of its four locations in 2026, leaving the concept with only one restaurant nationwide at 3631 SE Cornelius Pass Road in Hillsboro, Oregon, according to its restaurant locator . The closed locations include: Kennesaw, Georgia: Closed on November 22 at 1925 Cobb Parkway NW #120 after about 17 months in business, Tomorrow’s News Today reported. Peoria, Arizona: Closed on June 21 at 24759 N Lake Pleasant Parkway after operating for approximately 11 months, Your Valley reported. Pasadena, California: Closed in April at 1661 E Colorado Boulevard after around eight months in business, Tomorrow’s News Today reported. Cinnabon Swirl brought the two brands together, allowing customers to purchase Cinnabon’s cinnamon rolls and Carvel’s frozen desserts at the same location rather than visiting separate restaurants. The strategy also offered potential operational advantages for GoTo Foods. By combining the brands, the company aimed to create higher-productivity restaurants that could improve margins, expand customer reach, and support long-term growth. The concept also features exclusive menu items that customers cannot find at traditional Cinnabon or Carvel locations. Is Cinnabon Swirl shutting down? The Hillsboro restaurant was Cinnabon Swirl’s first location, which opened in May 2025, according to a company announcement . At the time, GoTo Foods said it planned to open more than 30 locations, with the three additional restaurants in Peoria, Kennesaw, and Pasadena opening later that year. “Consumers are increasingly seeking new and unique irresistible desserts, and Cinnabon Swirl was conceptualized to meet this evolving demand,” said Cinnabon Executive Chef Jennifer Holwill in the announcement. Although all three locations have since closed, GoTo Foods has not abandoned the concept entirely. The company plans to open another Cinnabon Swirl restaurant in Hawaii in 2027, according to Nation’s Restaurant News . GoTo Foods said several factors influence its decisions to close individual restaurants but did not disclose the specific reasons behind the recent Cinnabon Swirl shutdowns. The closures also do not mean the company is ending its broader Cinnabon and Carvel partnership. GoTo Foods operates approximately 31 Cinnabon and Carvel co-branded locations in the U.S. and has plans to open more in the future. These restaurants differ from the Cinnabon Swirl concept because they offer the two brands’ menus side by side rather than combining them into a single menu and standalone restaurant concept. Cinnabon Swirl closes nearly all locations. -lvinst- / Getty Images Dessert restaurant chains face ongoing struggles For dessert-focused brands, long-term success often depends on visit frequency because specialty treats are generally discretionary purchases rather than everyday necessities. Although premium desserts remain popular, consumers may be less likely to make frequent purchases when household budgets are under pressure. At the same time, rising labor, food, and occupancy costs can make it increasingly difficult for restaurant operators to maintain profitability across large store networks . The National Restaurant Association estimates that total expenses for an average restaurant increased 36% between 2019 and 2026. Average hourly earnings for restaurant employees have risen 41% since February 2020, while average wholesale food prices are up 35% over the same period. Those higher expenses have continued to put pressure on restaurant profitability. The National Restaurant Association reported that 33% of restaurant operators said their businesses were not profitable during the first half of 2026, highlighting the financial challenges facing the industry. Competition adds another challenge, as consumers have more options for occasional dessert purchases, ranging from specialty bakeries and frozen yogurt shops to established fast-food chains offering seasonal treats. Consumer spending habits are adding to those challenges, as some diners are cutting back on extras when eating out. The National Restaurant Association found that 34% of consumers reported ordering fewer add-ons, such as dessert and beverages, in its third-quarter 2026 survey. Additionally, 39% said they spent less at restaurants than in the previous quarter. “How often people realistically want dessert — is what ultimately determines which chains endure and which burn out,” said Business Insider Senior Reporter and industry expert Katherine Ortiz . “When too many concepts flood the market offering the same product for the same narrow occasion, the model goes stale, no matter how beloved the brand once was.” Cinnabon Swirl is not the only specialty dessert concept to experience difficulties maintaining its restaurant footprint. Several other chains have also closed locations in recent years. Here’s some of my previous coverage of dessert restaurant closures: The Cookie Factory closes all retail stores after 20 years Beard Papa’s quietly closes locations and exits multiple markets Orange Leaf frozen yogurt closes most locations While Cinnabon Swirl is not shutting down completely, the closure of three of its four restaurants highlights the challenges of expanding specialty dessert concepts . Its planned Hawaii opening in 2027 will provide another opportunity for GoTo Foods to test whether combining two established dessert brands can sustain a standalone restaurant model.
