title: Suze Orman warns of sobering retirement fact; urges Roth IRA fix
summary: As a viral SNL sketch and new University of Michigan data expose a widening eldercare burden on women, the bestselling personal finance author lays out a bold financial rule for siblings.
content: Most families assume that when aging parents need help, everyone will naturally pitch in. Yet personal finance author Suze Orman says a quiet financial trap is draining women’s retirement savings, a concern backed by new research from the University of Michigan and retirement rules from the IRS . In a Thanksgiving email message shared with TheStreet, Orman pointed to a viral “Saturday Night Live” commercial parody titled “ Sister ” — which racked up more than 9 million views on YouTube in just over a week — as a sharp, bittersweet mirror of reality. “It is fabulous because it is pitch-perfect in capturing the truth with humor,” Orman wrote in the message. “Women are typically the ones who step in and care for mom and dad in their later years. Sisters do the work. Brothers, not so much.” While the sketch drew laughs for depicting brothers coasting while their sister handles everything from medications to deep-cleaning Mom’s house, Orman warned that the real-world price tag is anything but funny. She also suggests a financial solution involving Roth IRAs that families can implement to rectify the imbalance. https://www.youtube.com/embed/-X9dxL17t1k University of Michigan data shows a widening caregiving gap Orman’s warning lands right alongside demographic findings from the University of Michigan Institute for Social Research , which found that U.S. women can now expect to spend about seven years of their adult lives caring for aging family members or friends, compared with roughly four years for men. Published in The Journals of Gerontology, Series B , the study revealed that the lifetime caregiving gap between women and men widened from two years in 2011 to three years in 2023. Crucially, lead author Vicki Freedman and co-author Crystal Yee To Ng found that men and women spend roughly the same amount of time, about 1.5 years, caring for an aging spouse or partner. Instead, the disparity is driven almost entirely by care provided to parents, grandparents, and extended relatives. “This study uses a demographic technique to calculate how many years of caregiving to an older adult a man or woman can expect to provide over their lifetimes if current rates hold into the future,” Freedman said in the university’s announcement . Orman also cited survey data showing that 62% of respondents view it as an unspoken expectation that daughters will step into the primary caregiver role. How caregiving compounds women’s retirement risk The hidden danger, Orman emphasized, is that eldercare often strikes just as women are trying to rebuild or maximize their retirement savings. “Women already lose out on valuable earnings when they take time off for child-rearing,” Orman wrote. “To compound those lost earnings, scaling back or stopping paid work to care for an aging adult compounds this harsh financial hit. It’s not just lifetime earnings, but may also impact Social Security benefits as well, given less time in a paid job contributing to Social Security.” That warning echoes broader retirement guidance Orman has issued for 2027, noting that stepping out of the workforce or cutting hours in your 50s and early 60s strips away peak earning years and the compound growth those contributions would have generated. To keep one sibling from bearing the entire burden alone, Orman urged caregivers to establish clear rules with their families: Split the logistics: Long-distance siblings can manage insurance paperwork, medical appointments, and mail-order prescription refills. Fund respite care: Family members who aren’t providing daily hands-on care can pay for hired help once or twice a week, or cover a housekeeper for the aging parent and the caregiving sibling. Compensate lost wages: “And for those families with the financial means, a sister who is providing substantial care should be paid for her work,” Orman wrote. “Especially if she scales back or quits a paying job.” Orman’s 2027 Roth IRA strategy for working caregivers For daughters and sisters who manage to keep working while carrying heavy caregiving duties, Orman proposed a specific financial fix: Siblings who benefit from that unpaid labor should pool their money to fund her Roth IRA. Under IRS rules, a saver must have enough earned income, either their own or a spouse’s if filing jointly, to qualify for a Roth IRA contribution, but the actual cash deposited into the account can come as a tax-free gift from siblings or other relatives. More Retirement: Annuities can be a retirement safety net to prevent outliving savings Vanguard flags a retirement fear built into 401(k) plans Suze Orman has a serious retirement warning for 2027 For the 2027 tax year, the IRS announced that the base annual IRA contribution limit remains $7,500, while savers age 50 and older can contribute up to $8,600, including the $1,100 catch-up allowance. Single filers can make the full contribution in 2027 with a modified adjusted gross income below $158,000, while married couples filing jointly qualify below $250,000. “With the new adjustment in place now, the IRS is giving taxpayers and employers the information needed to make retirement planning decisions for the year ahead,” the IRS stated in its 2027 retirement plan announcement . Orman’s bottom line for women carrying the family load this holiday season is for them to stop waiting for relatives to volunteer. They must proactively name the exact financial and practical support they need. “With no shame, no blame, and no hesitation, you are to tell everyone who benefits from your caregiving exactly how they need to support you,” Orman wrote. title: Consumers are rethinking who should control their money
summary: Consumers are asking different questions before putting money anywhere. The industry is still working out how to answer them.
content: Digital banking and payment apps changed what it feels like to manage money. The experience became faster, smoother, and accessible from a phone. What did not change was the structure underneath: an institution holds the asset, and the consumer holds a record of it. Those two things are not the same, and a growing number of consumers are beginning to understand the difference. Synapse’s collapse left nearly $160 million in fintech users’ funds inaccessible in 2024. Courts spent months on the insolvency process, and many customers were still waiting when it wrapped up. High-profile security incidents at large financial platforms pushed the concern further into view. It stopped being theoretical for many people. Also read: Michael Burry sees a serious problem Wall Street may be overlooking The question now moving through the financial industry is what that shift in expectations actually means for institutions and platforms competing for consumer deposits, trades, and assets. Trading platform Byrrgis entered that conversation with the launch of a non-custodial platform supporting Solana, Ethereum, BNB Chain, and Robinhood Chain, letting users trade across multiple networks without surrendering control of their assets. The launch is a direct response to a question more consumers are asking. How the definition of financial security is shifting Most people set up digital banking accounts without reading much past the initial screens. The features worked. The money moved. For years, that was enough. The scrutiny that followed came largely from customers who encountered a problem and discovered how the platform was actually structured as they tried to solve it. That standard is harder for institutions to meet than the old one. It is not enough to say funds are protected; more consumers want to see how, and what happens if that protection is ever tested. “Security used to mean ‘the institution will protect me,'” Tomer Sharoni, CEO of Addressable, told TheStreet. “Today, I believe it increasingly means ‘I can verify what’s happening.'” People ask different questions now before putting money somewhere. What happens to funds if the platform closes? How quickly can money actually be moved? Who has access to it besides the account holder? Five years ago, most consumers did not think to ask them. What institutions offer, and where the model has limits The case for institutional custody is not abstract. Banks have fraud departments, dispute processes, and deposit insurance frameworks that are backed by real legal structures. Many consumers have never needed any of that. The ones who have tend to understand why it exists. That infrastructure is not incidental to banking. It is a large part of its value, and for the vast majority of everyday financial activity, it still works. The limits of that model have been visible in the broader digital finance market. When platforms failed, customer funds held in custody were often treated as platform assets in bankruptcy rather than customer property. The protections that apply to bank deposits do not automatically extend to other financial accounts, and consumers operating in those spaces have often discovered this after the fact. “Being able to move, add, or get access to your assets is essential and is a minimum viable solution necessary for any financial product to work for anyone,” Al Qureshi, Co-founder and CEO of Black Lake Digital Markets, said to TheStreet. Most bank customers never stress-test what they have. They deposit money, run transactions, and that covers it. The harder questions about what happens when something breaks stay invisible for most people and usually only come up after something has already broken. Self-custody transfers control but it also transfers responsibility. Losing access to a private key without a backup, or approving a malicious transaction, can result in permanent loss of funds. AzmanL / Getty Images The risks consumers take on when they hold assets directly Self-custody transfers control but it also transfers responsibility. Losing access to a private key without a backup, or approving a malicious transaction, can result in permanent loss of funds. There is no fraud team to call and no dispute process available. “Most self-custody losses aren’t sophisticated hacks,” Sharoni said. “They’re people tricked into authorizing the theft themselves, through fake websites, look-alike addresses or fake support agents asking for a seed phrase.” The mechanics of self-custody are not especially difficult to explain. What makes it risky for most people is execution. Keeping private keys secure is a different skill than keeping a password secure. Spotting a fake interface before confirming a transaction requires a kind of pattern recognition most users have not had reason to build. Getting something wrong typically means the loss is permanent. That is the design problem non-custodial platforms have yet to fully solve. The tools exist for people with technical fluency. Getting them to work for a broader audience is a different challenge entirely, and it is the one that will determine how far the shift toward direct financial control actually goes. What non-custodial platforms are attempting to build The design challenge is combining the control of self-custody with the usability that consumers expect from modern financial apps. The two have historically been in tension. Platforms that prioritize user control often place a greater technical burden on users. Platforms built for ease of use typically take custody in return. Very few have managed both at scale. More Wall Street: Arista Networks stock gets fresh backing from Jim Cramer and Wall Street Oracle stock sinks as Wall Street confronts a $20 billion AI problem Wall Street just got a candid look at who is winning the AI race “We built Byrrgis because trading across chains was way more complicated than it needed to be,” Eric Andersson, Co-Founder of Byrrgis, said to TheStreet. “We wanted to make it easier without taking custody of consumers’ assets.” The assumption built into most financial platforms is that custody comes with the account. Users hand it over during sign-up and rarely revisit the question. What platforms like Byrrgis are testing is whether that ever had to be the case. The number of consumers asking about it has grown to the point that the question is worth taking seriously. How the pressure on custody is likely to reshape the industry Traditional financial institutions are not positioned to respond quickly. The regulatory requirements that protect consumers also limit the pace at which banks can restructure custody offerings or build new approaches to asset management. Banks are not unaware of what is happening. The constraints that slow them down also come with something newer platforms do not always have: a track record of being reachable when customers need help. That matters to a portion of their customer base, and those customers are not rushing anywhere. “Banks move slowly and are heavily regulated,” Qureshi said. “The solutions will come squarely from technology companies, and they will most likely be built on blockchains.” The more immediate competitive pressure falls on fintech companies and newer financial platforms, which operate in a faster-moving environment and compete directly for consumers who are already questioning custody arrangements. For those companies, whether to take custody or build for user control is a product decision with real market consequences. “Consumers will want more freedom to choose where they keep their assets, who holds them and how easily they can move them,” Andersson said. “That could push banks and fintechs to offer more flexibility.” What the last few years have made clear is that consumers are paying more attention to what custody actually means. Some of that comes from people who lost money. Some come from people who watched others lose money and started asking the same questions. The platform that can answer those questions convincingly and back it up with something concrete has an advantage that most financial providers are still figuring out how to build. title: Another holiday airline cancels all flights until 2027
summary: Holiday airline BeOnd has once again pushed back the restart of its flights.
content: With the consequences of the U.S. strike on Iran continuing to cause periodic flare-ups and retaliatory attacks around the entire Middle Eastern region, multiple airlines are unable to fly into cities like Dubai, Abu Dhabi, Doha and Riyadh. British Airways, KLM, Air France, Delta, United and American have all recently pushed back the restart date of their flights as volatility in the region makes resuming service only to potentially have to cancel it again a few weeks later too risky and expensive. BeOnd, a boutique airline that began operations in November 2023 with a business model of selling flights to The Maldives from Middle Eastern and European capitals, saw a sharp dropoff in traveler numbers amid airspace closures following February 2026. Flights from European cities like Milan and Zürich flew to Velana International Airport in Malé through a stopover in Dubai International. BeOnd again pushes back restart of Maldives flights Calling off its flights and temporarily grounding its fleet immediately after the start of the war in Iran, BeOnd has also been forced to repeatedly push back its restart date further into the future as the geopolitical instability set off by the attack shows little signs of stabilizing. The latest travel update put out by the all-business airline says that “scheduled flights will not operate in December 2026” due to “current conditions in the region.” The most recent instability comes from repeated Houthi attacks on Saudi ports and other targets in the Red Sea. A note stating that the “majority” of “scheduled flights from 1 December to 31 December 2026” will not take place leaves open the possibility that some limited or chartered services could be run at the last minute. Airlines tha t shut down in November 2026: Fly Beena: At the end of November , Egyptian hotel group Travco Group pulled out of plans to launch an airline to fly tourists from several European cities to Egyptian resorts . Fly Beena’s plans were initially announced in April through an early investment from the conglomerate. Global Airlines: The airline startup, launched by holiday travel platform Holiday Swap founder James Asquith, was shut down when the High Court of Justice in London issued a winding-up petition on Nov. 4 . Magnicharters: After canceling its flights for a period that was initially supposed to last for two weeks, the Mexican low-cost airline was officially declared bankrupt by a court at the beginning of November . AlbaStar: The Spanish airline based in Mallorca announced that it has “made the difficult decision to temporarily suspend” all its flights in November and through the rest of 2026. As with extended travel waiver in place since BeOnd first canceled its flights last spring, passengers who booked travel and chosen not to receive a refund can continue to extend it to a future date or request the refund at any point. BeOnd is currently unable to run its flights to The Maldives amid Middle Eastern instability and the war in Iran. Michael Derrer Fuchs / Getty Images What is happening with BeOnd flights for the rest of 2026, refund options A few flights to Zürich, Munich, and Milan ran in October 2026 during a brief lull in hostilities around Dubai before BeOnd ultimately suspended services again. Prior to the start of the war, BeOnd had also been planning to launch its first direct route to The Maldives from the U.S. but those plans were put on indefinite hold when its U.S. partner New Pacific Airlines ceased operations in November 2025. While the carrier is privately owned and so not required to publish regular earnings reports, chief executive Tero Taskila had previously sent an internal memo acknowledging that BeOnd is behind on salary payments for its staff. Future funding rounds are also contingent on its ability to run flights. It is not immediately clear how BeOnd’s immediate liquidity challenges were addressed as months passed and the situation has not changed for it to resume its business model of flying to The Maldives from and through the Middle East. title: Low-cost airline Norse Atlantic cancels flights, appears to shut down
summary: The budget airline had previously warned investors that it was in a "critical financial situation."
content: Norse Atlantic Airways, a Norwegian low-cost airline that once ran dozens of routes between the East Coast of the U.S. and different European capitals, appears to have shut down, as all flights initially scheduled for Wednesday, Nov. 25, were canceled. The budget airline that began operations and went public on the Oslo Stock Exchange in 2021 saw its shares plunge by more than 53% by closing hours on Nov. 25 after the carrier issued a statement warning investors and the general public that its “financial situation is critical.” In its last earnings quarter published at the end of June, Norse reported debt of more than $70.6 million USD. The spike in jet fuel prices due to the war in Iran played a significant part in the spiraling debt. “No assurances”: Norse Atlantic Airways cancels November flights “Norse is also engaged in discussions with selected parties on short-term financing,” the statement read further. “However, there can be no assurances that such discussions will result in a viable solution.” While Norse did not initially specify how much financing it would need to cover immediate liquidity problems or when it would need to shut down operations, flights scheduled for Nov. 26 now appear to have disappeared from FlightRadar24. Related: Ryanair exits entire market Two flights that Norse was scheduled to operate for Pakistan International Airlines through a wet-lease agreement with its Boeing 787 planes have been called off 24 hours before the scheduled departure, CNBC reported . The Pakistani flag carrier named “an unexpected operational suspension” as the reason PK786 from London to Islamabad and PK710 from Manchester to Lahore were called off. The Norse Atlantic flight from London Gatwick to Orlando, Z0 783, is also marked as canceled for Nov. 26. Norse Atlantic is facing a liquidity crisis amid a spike in jet fuel costs. Mrkit99 / Getty Images Norse stock plummets as airline warns of “critical” financial situation Norse has not issued an official statement on the cancellations, so it is not immediately clear if they mark a full or partial collapse. Low-cost competitors had previously canceled flights for a few weeks to save costs during restructuring or unprofitable periods. The Norse website remains up and allows customers to purchase flight tickets, including ones marketed through a seasonal Black Friday promotion. Two flights from JFK to London Gatwick and Rome Fiumicino were phased out in October 2026; the carrier also cut 75 jobs in the spring as part of its stated effort to reduce its expenses by $50 million by 2027. title: One of the coolest small airports in the U.S. is not where you think
summary: The new terminal Patrick Leahy Burlington International Airport opened earlier this year after a $68 million expansion.
content: Vermont, a state known for everything from its world-class ski resorts to its maple syrup and craft beer industries, is in a unique geographical position at the very tip of the northeast of the U.S. — a 90-mile border with Canada that runs across forests, Lake Champlain, and the Missisquoi River to the north and shared borders with Massachusetts, New Hampshire or New York further south. According to statistics from the state’s tourism industry, just over 78% of the 15.6 million out-of-state visitors who came to Vermont last year drove in by car from or through neighboring states like Massachusetts, New Hampshire or New York. While this makes the state an overwhelmingly drive market for visitors, Patrick Leahy International Airport (BTV) in Burlington has recently gone through a $68 million terminal concourse expansion financed by government grants and spending secured by the namesake former senator amid the city and the region’s growth. As part of the airport expansion project known locally as Project NexT, the new 60,000-square-foot concourse added to the north section of the terminal opened to visitors in March 2026. The main airport in Vermont has an awesome observation deck for plane spotters The reworked terminal adds four new gates with passenger boarding bridges to accommodate larger aircraft like the Boeing 737 and Airbus A320 and is a light-filled space featuring floor-to-ceiling windows with runway views and warm natural wood in a linear interconnected layout that gives it a distinctly Vermont look. The Burlington airport observation area has both an outdoor deck and an indoor space. Veronika Bondarenko To meet power demand and hit net-zero goals in the coming decades, the airport also uses 32 geothermal wells drilled 600 feet underground that heat and cool the building alongside solar energy. Related: Three iconic New York City chains come to major airport But as someone who visited the renovated airport at the end of October, I found the new observation deck was by far the coolest part of the space. Accessible pre-security to anyone who comes there from 7 a.m. to 5 p.m. on weekdays, the third-floor observation area has both an indoor and outdoor area to watch planes landing on the airport’s two runways alongside the Camel’s Hump and Mount Mansfield of the state’s legendary Green Mountains. Somewhat similar in style to the rooftop of the TWA Hotel in New York City, the observation deck attracts local avgeeks looking to plane-spot during the day while being architecturally envisioned as a spot to be rented out for corporate happy hours and other events during later hours. The new North Terminal at Burlington International Airport opened in March 2026. Veronika Bondarenko The future of Burlington International Airport: Record passenger numbers and more terminal plans in the works This wave of airport investment in Vermont is pleasing to see. The approximately 160,000 departures and arrivals in October 2026 have set a new record for a regional airport that serves as the main gateway to a state many are looking to visit. The first international commercial flight to Burlington since 2018, when a route to Toronto was discontinued, also returned this month with a Bermudair flight to the sunny destination’s capital city; the terminal expansion coincides with the goal of growing the network of international flights.
